74.0.s.en: (1) God's silence in the face of the cruelty of the wicked

74.0.0.en: 1- O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever? why doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture?

74.0.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm reproaches God, because He allowed a severe affliction for His people, and by this it appears that He has rejected His people, and when the trial grew long the writer said, with sorrow, that he feels the affliction continuing and extending as if it were for ever. And God does not reject His people except because of their sins, for He allows the affliction to chasten them so that they repent, and if they repent He forgives them and lifts the affliction from them.

74.0.2.en: 2- And the writer asks with sorrow, as if saying to God, Why do You show Your anger against Your people, who are the sheep You shepherd? And the anger of God is a consuming fire from which black smoke comes out and covers the people of God, as a warning to them so that they repent, otherwise the fire will consume them and they will perish. But the beautiful thing is that he says "the sheep of thy pasture", that is, You are the One responsible for us, confident of the love of God which does not neglect His children.

74.1.0.en: 2- Remember thy congregation, which thou hast purchased of old; the rod of thine inheritance, which thou hast redeemed; this mount Zion, wherein thou hast dwelt.

74.1.1.en: In his need the writer of the Psalm did not demand his needs from God, but reminded Him of His love for His people, and pointed to important matters in God's relationship with His people:

74.1.2.en: 1- The people of God are His congregation belonging to Him, and not to another.

74.1.3.en: 2- God is the One who purchased His people, and called His name upon them.

74.1.4.en: 3- God's relationship with His people is very old, from the days of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

74.1.5.en: 4- God redeemed His people when He brought them out of the land of Egypt, for He killed the firstborn of Egypt, but when He looked at the blood smeared on the doors, the angel passed over, and did not kill the firstborn of Israel, that is, He redeemed them by the blood of the lamb, which is a reference to the blood of Christ.

74.1.6.en: 5- Israel comprises twelve tribes, which the writer gathers here by saying "the rod of thine inheritance", that is, they are all God's inheritance on earth, since they are the only people who believed in God at that time.

74.1.7.en: 6- God Himself dwelt in the midst of His people in Jerusalem, that is, Zion, and blessed this people. By all these remembrances the writer moves the heart of God to compassion on His people, to deliver them from the trials they are passing through.

74.2.0.en: 3- Lift up thy feet unto the perpetual desolations; even all that the enemy hath done wickedly in the sanctuary.

74.2.2.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm calls upon God to intervene quickly for the sake of His Temple which has been destroyed, and because of the horror of the destruction he describes it as perpetual desolations, that is, that it was severely ruined, that is, that it will not be rebuilt for ever, but of course God is able to rebuild it. And he describes what the enemies did as destruction of the whole, that is, a total destruction, by his saying "all that the enemy hath done wickedly", so the need for God's intervention is great. All this is a prophecy about the destruction of the Temple, as we mentioned in the introduction, in the days of Babylon, or the Greeks, or the Romans.

74.2.3.en: 2- The enemy is Satan who destroys the human soul, and therefore the Psalm calls upon God to hasten to the help of man, and this was accomplished in the fullness of time by the Incarnation of Christ, to restore man as a temple of the Holy Spirit after Satan had destroyed him.

74.3.0.en: 4- Thine enemies roar in the midst of thy congregations; they set up their ensigns for signs. 5- A man was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees. 6- But now they break down the carved work thereof at once with axes and hammers. Thy congregations (ma'hadak): thy dwelling, that is, the Tabernacle of Meeting. Hammers (ma'awil): plural of mi'wal, a strong iron tool with which rock is broken, or the ground is dug, or things are smashed.

74.3.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm likens the voices of the enemies who will attack the Temple to lions, and their voices are the roaring of lions, that is, their voices are loud, proclaiming their victory over Your people, as if they had done great signs; because they forgot that Almighty God is long-suffering, and although He chastens His people by the destruction of the Temple, He will take vengeance on the enemies, and will rebuild the Temple.

74.3.2.en: 2- He describes their cruelty in smashing and destroying the Temple as if they carried axes and cut down thick trees; because they broke all the carved woodwork that adorned the Temple (2 Kgs 25:8-17; Jer 52:12-23).

74.4.0.en: 7- They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground. 8- They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land.

74.4.1.en: The synagogues of God (ma'ahid): the Jewish synagogues which the Jews established from the second century before Christ in the various countries to read the Holy Scriptures in them and explain them and pray. They continued until the days of Christ, and in the apostolic age. As for the sacrifices, they were offered only in the Temple in Jerusalem.

74.4.2.en: 1- The enemies entered the Temple of God, and defiled it with their feet; because it is not permitted for pagans to enter the Temple, and their wicked hand stretched out to burn the Temple with fire, and they tried to kill the Jews. This is what happened at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar at the Babylonian captivity in 587 BC, and it was repeated at the hand of Antiochus the Great in the second century before Christ, who burned the doors of the Temple, while in 70 AD Titus the Roman destroyed the Temple completely.

74.4.3.en: 2- The hand of the enemies stretched out to destroy the Jewish synagogues spread throughout the whole earth. All this shows the cruelty of the enemies toward the people of God, and God kept silent over all they did; because He intended to chasten His people so that they would repent.

74.5.0.en: 9- We see not our signs: there is no more any prophet: neither is there among us any that knoweth how long.

74.5.1.en: 1- The Jews became in the darkness of sin and went far from God, and the chastenings mentioned in the previous verses came upon them, besides that they did not see the signs of God, nor prophets declaring the voice of God to them, although there were prophets and signs, but the Jews did not understand them, and did not obey the prophets, but considered them wicked, and rose against them and killed them, like Isaiah whom they sawed asunder, and Jeremiah whom they stoned, and Ezekiel whom they killed.

74.5.2.en: 2- This verse may be a prophecy about what would happen after the crucifixion of Christ and His redemption, for from that time until now the Jews have seen no signs, nor prophets. And they are still waiting for the Messiah, and do not know when; because they rejected the awaited Messiah when He became incarnate and died to redeem them.

74.5.3.en: If you see afflictions passing over you, examine yourself instead of murmuring or despairing, for your sins may be the cause, and hasten to repentance and you will receive God's blessings and mercies; because He loves you.

74.6.0.en: 10- O God, how long shall the adversary reproach? shall the enemy blaspheme thy name for ever? 11- Why withdrawest thou thy hand, even thy right hand? pluck it out of thy bosom.

74.6.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm asks God, and says to Him, Do You not see the adversaries, and the enemies insulting Your name, and reproaching us, because we are Your people! Why do You keep silent, and prolong Your longsuffering? And how long will You hide Your hand and Your right hand, or Your power? For I believe that You are able to destroy all the power of the enemies. And You are jealous and do not accept this reproach and this insult. And it is clear that the writer of the Psalm is appealing for God's mercies, that He may have compassion on His people, and intervene, and accept their repentance, and rescue them.

74.6.2.en: 2- These two verses are a prophecy about the burning of the Temple and the Babylonian captivity, or the assault of Antiochus, or the Jews' resistance to Christ. So the writer of the Psalm asks God to rebuild His Temple, and declare the truth, and the only Son be glorified as happened in the Resurrection.

74.6.3.en: 3- Every human soul that suffers from the wars of the devil calls upon God with these two verses, that He may intervene and rescue it, and lift it up from its weaknesses.

74.7.0.en: 12- For God is my King of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth.

74.7.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm relies on his relationship with God that He is his King all his life, so he always trusts in Him, and He is the One who protects him and supports him, and not only in his life, but also from of old with his fathers and forefathers; for God has shepherded His people from the days of the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and He alone is able to save him and his people from the hard afflictions they are passing through. So he speaks with God with boldness that He may have mercy on him, and rescue him as He did from of old with His people, such as bringing them out of Egypt by the ten plagues, then dividing the Red Sea, and the crossing of His people, and the drowning of the Egyptians.

74.7.2.en: 2- Perhaps the writer of the Psalm speaks in the spirit of prophecy about the salvation of Christ in the fullness of time, which He will accomplish in Jerusalem, in the midst of the earth.

74.8.0.en: 13- Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength: thou brakest the heads of the dragons in the waters.

74.8.1.en: Dragons: ancient sea monsters that became extinct, and they used to attack ships and their passengers.

74.8.2.en: Thou brakest in pieces (radadta): thou broke. Leviathan: a sea monster that has heads, and is very ravenous, and has become extinct, and some say that it may be the crocodile found at the sources of the Nile.

74.8.3.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm reminds God of His former works with His people, for He is the One who divided the Red Sea so that His people crossed on dry land in the midst of the sea, and broke the heads of the dragons, by whom he means the great soldiers and heroes in Pharaoh's army. And Pharaoh was drowned with all his mighty men, and He broke in pieces the heads of leviathan, by whom he means Pharaoh, so he was drowned, and the corpses of his army came up on the shore of the wilderness of Sinai, and instead of his devouring the people of God, the people devoured him, that is, they triumphed over him, and he became food for the people of the wilderness, who are the wild beasts of the wilderness.

74.8.4.en: 2- The dragons and leviathan are also the demons whom Christ breaks in the water of Baptism, and strips of their authority over His children, so that the baptized are freed from the nature inclined to evil, and are born with the new nature that is inclined to life with God. For Christ the Savior by His redemption divided the waters, and broke the power of the demons, and gave His children victory and authority over serpents and scorpions, and all the power of the enemy.

74.9.0.en: 15- Thou didst cleave the fountain and the flood: thou driedst up mighty rivers.

74.9.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm also reminded God of His ancient works when He cleaved the fountain of water, and the waters flowed from the rock when Moses struck it. And this was repeated many times in the wilderness of Sinai. And he reminded God also that He dried up the river Jordan when the priests in the days of Joshua the son of Nun entered with the Ark of the Covenant, and the waters dried up under their feet, and the people of God crossed over and entered the land of Canaan. So God, who is able to cleave the waters and dry up the rivers, is of course able to rescue His people from their enemies.

74.9.2.en: 2- The gushing waters and floods symbolize the souls of the Gentiles who believed in Christ, and from whom gifts and works overflowed because of the Holy Spirit in them. And at the same time God dried up the flowing rivers, which symbolize the Jews who refused to believe in Christ, so the works of God in them dried up because of the hardness of their hearts.

74.10.0.en: 16- The day is thine, the night also is thine: thou hast prepared the light and the sun.

74.10.2.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm addresses God, and reminds Him that He is the Creator of day and night, and the sun, and all the planets, and the One who orders the succession of day and night, and likewise the succession of summer and winter, and all the seasons of the year, and He is the One who sets the boundaries of nature in the movement of the sea, and the whole earth, and all the planets. For God sets boundaries and order for all His creatures; and consequently His power is great, and He is able to rescue His people; because everything is in His hand.

74.10.3.en: 3- Day and light symbolize the righteous and those who fear God, and night symbolizes those far from God, occupied with sin, for which darkness is fitting. But the sun symbolizes the Sun of Righteousness, that is, Christ who shines upon the whole world, so He lights the places that were dark, and makes them light, that is, God works in all, those near Him and those far, so that all may believe, and those far may repent, and live with Him, and so be saved.

74.10.4.en: Meditate every day on the power of God in whose hand is the authority over all creation; so that your heart may be reassured, and that you may fear Him, and keep away from sin, and then God will reveal His beauty to you, and you will enjoy fellowship with Him.

74.11.0.en: 18- Remember this, that the enemy hath reproached, O Lord, and that the foolish people have blasphemed thy name.

74.11.1.en: Reproached ('ayyara): showed his faults and attributed ugliness and deficiency to him.

74.11.2.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm calls upon God, showing the impudence of the enemies who reproach His people, and attribute weakness to their God, and even insult the name of the holy God, and consequently he asks Him for quick intervention, to defend His great name, and rescue His people from the hands of their enemies; for the enemies from of old have boasted of their pagan gods, and spoken arrogantly against the name of the God of Israel.

74.11.3.en: 2- This verse also applies to what happened with Christ, whom the Jews insulted, and whose rulers insulted Him, and accused Him of wicked accusations, that He deals with the prince of the demons, and that He is a blasphemer and an evildoer, and a glutton and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and harlots.

74.12.0.en: 19- O deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude of the wicked: forget not the congregation of thy poor for ever.

74.12.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm continues to appeal for God's mercies and compassion, and likens the people of God, or His Church in the New Testament, to the dove which cannot defend itself, and which loves quietness and peace, and likens Satan and all the wicked to the beast that attacks the children of God.

74.12.2.en: 2- And he also likens the people of God to a flock of the poor, that is, a whole company of the poor and weak, unable to defend itself. But the beautiful thing in the matter is that he calls them "thy poor", that is, that they belong to God, and God cannot forget the one who has relied on Him, so He defends him and saves him from his enemies.

74.13.0.en: 20- Have respect unto the covenant: for the dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty.

74.13.1.en: Dark places (muzlimat): the places that are dark.

74.13.2.en: He also reminds God of His covenant with His people which He made with the fathers of old, and which He sealed with blood in the days of Moses; that He would be a God to His people, and they would obey His commandments. That is, that He is the One responsible for defending His people and caring for them. And at the same time he shows God that the earth has been filled with injustice, and much injustice is known in the darkness, and by this he means every injustice that has befallen the people of God; therefore God's quick intervention is needed to lift this injustice from His people.

74.14.0.en: 21- O let not the oppressed return ashamed: let the poor and needy praise thy name.

74.14.1.en: As a result of God's intervention and His rescue of His people, His children praise Him and glorify Him, because He gave them victory over their enemies, and they trampled shame underfoot. And to obtain God's mercies, contrition, that is, humility, is necessary, and the feeling of need as the poor and needy feel. For this is the shortest way to the heart of God, to obtain His mercies.

74.15.0.en: 22- Arise, O God, plead thine own cause: remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee daily. 23- Forget not the voice of thine enemies: the tumult of those that rise up against thee increaseth continually. Thine enemies (adhdadak): plural of thy adversary, and the adversary is the opponent and the resister.

74.15.1.en: Tumult (dajij): a loud and disturbing noise.

74.15.2.en: 1- He closes the Psalm with the request for God to arise after His silence for a period, to plead His cause, by which he means the cause and the complaint of His people before Him; that He may do them justice. And he said "thine own cause" because the people of God belong to Him, so their cause is His cause. For He is the judge and the defender at the same time of His people.

74.15.3.en: 2- What calls God to quick intervention is the enemies' continuing to reproach His holy name, and showing this with impudence, cruelty and violence, which he expresses by tumult. These enemies deserve punishment for the following:

74.15.4.en: a- That they are fools, that is, pagans, refusing to know God.

74.15.5.en: b- That they resist God (thine enemies).

74.15.6.en: c- They speak with violence and pride, raising their voices with tumult.

74.15.7.en: 3- And the writer of the Psalm does not mean to take vengeance on the enemies, but asks with humility for the glorification of the name of God which the enemies have insulted.

74.15.8.en: When you speak with another, show your concern for him, and not for yourself, and you will win his love and sympathy, and he will be ready to feel for you and help you.

74.15.9.en: God the Chastener and Rewarder: to the chief Musician, Al-taschith, a Psalm of Asaph, a song. "Unto thee, O God, do we give thanks, unto thee do we give thanks: for that thy name is near" (v. 1). Introduction:

74.15.10.en: 1- Its writer: a- Asaph, as the title mentions.

74.15.11.en: b- David wrote it, then gave it to Asaph to sing before the Temple.

74.15.13.en: a- There is an opinion that David wrote it when the angel stood in the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite and stopped the plague. So he thanked God who is just and merciful at the same time (2 Sam 24:1-17).

74.15.14.en: b- And there is another opinion that David wrote the Psalm after the death of Saul, and his becoming king.

74.15.15.en: 3- This Psalm glorifies the just God, the Controller of all, who by His power punishes the wicked and rewards the righteous.

74.15.16.en: 4- There is a completion between (Ps 74) and (Ps 75), for the first reproaches God for the delay of His intervention to rescue His people, and in this Psalm he thanks God for His intervention, and the rewarding of His children.

74.15.17.en: 5- There is a resemblance between this Psalm and the Psalm that follows it, and also the prayer of Hannah the mother of Samuel (1 Sam 2:1-10), for both speak of the just God.

74.15.18.en: 6- This Psalm calls every person to beware of sin because of its severe punishment (v. 8), and alerts him to prepare for eternity (vv. 9, 10).

74.15.19.en: 7- This Psalm in its title has "Al-taschith" (Do not destroy), which was a musical tune known at that time.

74.15.20.en: 8- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
